title: Register & Style
description: Master register and style for Grade 11: formal vs informal register, and academic, journalistic, literary and business styles — with bilingual notes, examples, practice and tests.

topics.title: Formal vs Informal Register
topics.concept:
Register runs on a scale from very informal to very formal. The markers:

MarkerInformalFormal
Wordsget, kids, a lot of, ask forreceive, children, numerous, request
ContractionsI'm, won'tI am, will not
Slang/idiomcool, no big dealexcellent, not significant
Sentencesshort, personal (I, you)longer, impersonal (one, it is…)
Phrasal verbsfind out, give updiscover, abandon

Formal English prefers full words, the passive or impersonal voice, and precise vocabulary; informal English is relaxed, personal and uses contractions and phrasal verbs. Neither is 'better' — each fits its situation.

topics.title: Styles: Academic, Journalistic, Literary, Business
topics.concept:
Beyond register, writing has a style shaped by its purpose:

StyleFeatures
Academicimpersonal, passive, nominalised, hedged ('it appears that…'), evidence-based
Journalisticshort sentences, active voice, present tense, catchy lead, plain words
Literaryvaried sentence length, imagery, figurative language, rhythm
Businessclear, polite, direct, courteous formulae ('We are pleased to…')

The same fact reads very differently in each: an academic report 'analyses findings', a newspaper 'breaks the story', a novel 'paints a scene', and a business letter 'requests action'. Recognising and producing each style is the mark of an advanced writer.

examples.problem: Which style? It was found that pollution levels had risen significantly.
examples.solution: Academic — impersonal, passive ('It was found'), hedged and evidence-based.

examples.problem: Which style? Floods hit the city today as rivers burst their banks.

recap: Literary: imagery, varied rhythm; Business: clear, polite, direct

intro.en: Register is the level of formality you choose for a situation; style is the overall manner of expression. You would not write to a friend the way you write a job application. A skilled writer reads the audience and the purpose, then dials the language up or down — formal or relaxed, academic or journalistic — to fit perfectly.
intro.hi: Register वह औपचारिकता-स्तर है जो आप किसी स्थिति के लिए चुनते हैं; style अभिव्यक्ति का समग्र ढंग है। जैसे आप किसी मित्र को लिखते हैं वैसे आप नौकरी का आवेदन नहीं लिखेंगे। कुशल लेखक श्रोता और उद्देश्य पढ़कर भाषा को ऊपर-नीचे करता है — औपचारिक या सहज, शैक्षणिक या पत्रकारीय — ताकि वह बिल्कुल फिट बैठे।

real_life.situation:
Same message, two registers:

Informal: Hey, can you send me that file ASAP? Thanks!

Formal: Could you kindly forward the document at your earliest convenience? Thank you.
real_life.why: The informal version suits a friend; the formal one suits a manager or a stranger. Same meaning, different register — choosing correctly is the difference between sounding appropriate and sounding out of place.

reading.passage: The same flood was reported three ways. The newspaper announced: "Disaster strikes — thousands flee rising waters." The scientist wrote: "Rainfall in the region exceeded historical averages, resulting in widespread inundation." The novelist remembered: "The brown river crept like a thief, swallowing the fields it had once nourished." Each writer told the truth, yet each chose a style to suit a different reader.

questions.q: Identify the journalistic line and two of its features.
questions.answer: 'Disaster strikes — thousands flee rising waters.' — short, active, present tense, attention-grabbing.

questions.q: What makes the scientist's sentence academic?
questions.answer: It is impersonal and precise, uses nominalisation ('inundation') and an objective, evidence-based tone.

questions.q: How does the novelist's sentence show literary style?
questions.answer: It uses imagery and a simile ('crept like a thief') and personification ('swallowing the fields').
